verdicts.why: A technical term for a variable in an expression; it names a mathematical role and takes no attitude toward it.
Plainly names the act of protecting against attack; no approval or contempt rides on choosing it over 'protect' or 'defend'.
In the glossed sense it means to remark on something, a neutral act of commenting; the social 'be noticed' of the sentences is a different sense.
Names whoever originates something without judging them; the feeling in the sentences belongs to 'vexation' and 'happiness', not to 'source'.
A cited publication is named plainly; the word carries no view of the publication's worth.
Whatever inspires later work is described, not rated; 'source' in this sense is as plain as 'origin'.
A technical term for an input process in a system, with no attitude attached.
A facility where something can be obtained is named without approval or dismissal.
A reservoir of infection is an unpleasant referent, but the word is the plain epidemiological term and takes no side.
Marks on a surface representing language are named plainly; nothing about choosing 'writing' over 'script' or 'text' expresses attitude.
An author's collected works are named neutrally; 'her writings' says nothing about their quality.
The plain verb for acquiring by exchange; its neighbour 'purchase' differs in register, not in judgement.
Saying a sum will buy something states purchasing power as fact, with no attitude toward the thing or the sum.
In the glossed sense the word names a piece of work as a product of exertion; any praise or irony ('her finest effort', 'a feeble effort') comes from the modifier and context, not the noun itself.
The plainest possible verb for bringing something to a close; no attitude toward what is ended.
A dent left by pressing is a physical description with no judgement.
An imitation of a person's manner is named neutrally; whether the imitation is affectionate or mocking is not in the word.
A printed or engraved mark is a technical referent named without attitude.
The act of pressing one surface onto another is a plain physical description.
A print run is a publishing term with no evaluative charge.
A dental mould is a technical referent; the word judges nothing.
A factor that sways what one does is named neutrally; whether the influence is good or bad is left to context, as the sentences show.
Causing an effect without direct effort is described, not judged; it lacks the manipulative charge of a word like 'pull' or 'string-pulling'.
A territory held by a state is named in the plain legal-political term; ownership is the meaning, not an attitude beyond it.
Self-command is an admired trait, but 'possession' names it as plainly as 'composure' does; the approval belongs to the trait, not to the word.
